name: Tailender Tom Offline Knowledge Base
purpose: Offline Q&A, troubleshooting, and guidance for Christian field recording teams.
sourceSummary: Built from Dan's uploaded Rekordo/field recording training materials.
Uses neutral Christian field recording language.
Designed to run offline inside the Tailender Tracks PWA.

items.question: How do I know this is the right heart language?
items.answer: Check what people use at home, with family, and when telling stories. Do not rely only on a trade language, website, or outsider label. Ask local believers, community contacts, and speakers whether this dialect sounds natural and acceptable.
actions: Mark facts as Confirmed / Likely / Unknown

items.question: What language name should I enter?
items.answer: Enter the name local people use first. Add other spellings, government names, ISO code if known, and any names outsiders use.

items.question: What if I am not sure about the dialect?
items.answer: Do not guess. Mark the dialect as Unknown or Likely, then record a short word list or sample story and ask trusted local listeners whether it matches their speech variety.

items.question: Should I check if recordings already exist?
items.answer: Yes. Check whether Scripture, songs, older recordings, or partner materials already exist. This prevents duplicate work and helps you choose the best content gap.

items.question: What cultural notes should I collect?
items.answer: Look for family structure, authority, fears, felt needs, religious background, local stories, proverbs, songs, and objects that may help or hinder communication.

items.question: What does confirmed, likely, and unknown mean?
items.answer: Confirmed means a trusted local source or direct observation supports it. Likely means it seems true but needs checking. Unknown means the team should not build a major decision on it yet.

items.question: Why do we ask about literacy?
items.answer: Literacy affects whether audio, printed scripts, picture books, QR codes, or listening groups will work best. Oral learners may need short, natural, repeated audio rather than text-heavy resources.

items.question: How should I write religious background notes?
items.answer: Write respectfully and factually. Note what local people believe, what terms may confuse them, and whether there are churches, believers, or other religious influences nearby.

items.question: Who should be listed as a community contact?
items.answer: List trusted people who can verify language, help with speakers, explain culture, or connect the team with local churches and leaders. Include only safe contact details.

items.question: What map notes are useful?
items.answer: Write villages, regions, roads, rivers, mountains, and boundaries that may affect dialects or travel. Natural barriers often matter for speech variety and access.

items.question: How do I choose the right content?
items.answer: Start with the audience and ministry purpose. Choose Bible stories, Gospel messages, testimonies, songs, discipleship lessons, children’s lessons, or help messages that fit the listeners and local situation.

items.question: Should we translate word-for-word?
items.answer: Usually no. Preserve biblical truth and meaning, but shape the wording so it sounds natural in the target language. Ask, 'How would a wise local person say this clearly?'

items.question: What are Christianese words?
items.answer: Christianese words are church words that may sound familiar to Christians but unclear to listeners. Words like grace, repent, kingdom, born again, sacrifice, and eternal life may need careful local explanation.

items.question: How do I choose a good speaker?
items.answer: Choose someone with clear natural speech, local acceptance, patience, availability, and a voice that listeners will trust. Reading ability helps, but natural speech and acceptability may matter more.

items.question: Do we need consent before recording?
items.answer: Yes. Before recording, confirm the person understands how their voice may be used, where it may be shared, whether their name may be public, and any restrictions.

items.question: When do we need theological review?
items.answer: Use theological review before recording or publishing Gospel, Bible teaching, discipleship, or Scripture-based content, especially when the script is adapted or newly written.

items.question: Why include a local church or partner?
items.answer: Local partners help verify language, culture, speaker acceptability, follow-up, and real ministry use after the recording is shared.

items.question: What should be in the equipment checklist?
items.answer: Include recorder, microphone, headphones, batteries, charger, memory cards, cables, wind protection, laptop if needed, backup drive, labels, and consent/forms.

items.question: What is a backup plan?
items.answer: A backup plan says how you will protect original recordings before leaving the site. Use two copies when possible, on different devices or drives.

items.question: Why plan sharing before recording?
items.answer: Planning sharing early helps choose the right length, format, language, titles, and follow-up method. A recording is not finished until listeners can actually receive it.

items.question: What is room tone and why record it?
items.answer: Room tone is 20–30 seconds of quiet sound in the recording place. It helps editors understand the background noise and can help with noise reduction or smooth edits.

items.question: Should I do a test recording first?
items.answer: Yes. Record a short test, listen with headphones, check volume, noise, microphone position, and speaker comfort before the full session.

items.question: What does clipping mean?
items.answer: Clipping means the audio is too loud and distorted. Move the microphone slightly, lower input gain, or ask the speaker to speak naturally but not directly blast the mic.

items.question: What if the recording is too quiet?
items.answer: Move the microphone closer, raise input gain carefully, check the mic connection, and make a new test. Do not just hope editing will fix it.

items.question: What if there is background noise?
items.answer: Stop and identify the source: fan, generator, children, animals, wind, traffic, jewelry, chairs, or phones. Fix what you can before recording again.

items.question: How do I handle wind noise?
items.answer: Move indoors or behind a wind block, use a windscreen, turn the mic away from direct wind, and record a new test before continuing.

items.question: What do I do when the speaker makes a mistake?
items.answer: Pause, mark the mistake in notes, let the speaker restart from a natural sentence break, and keep the session calm. Do not shame the speaker.

items.question: What if the speaker is nervous?
items.answer: Slow down. Explain the process, record a practice line, encourage natural speech, and let a trusted helper sit nearby if culturally appropriate.

items.question: When should I back up the files?
items.answer: Back up original recordings before leaving the location. Originals may be irreplaceable, so do not wait until later if a copy can be made now.

items.question: What should I write in the recording session log?
items.answer: Write date, location, speaker, script section, equipment, file names, take numbers, best takes, noise problems, retakes, playback check, and backup status.

items.question: What is the difference between a track and a program?
items.answer: A track is one audio item. A program is the organized final set of tracks with titles, order, metadata, and purpose.

items.question: How should I order tracks?
items.answer: Put tracks in the order listeners should hear them. Keep story flow, teaching sequence, worship items, and introductions clear.

items.question: Why is missing metadata a problem?
items.answer: Missing titles, language, speaker, Scripture references, permissions, or track order can slow review, publishing, sharing, and future reuse.

items.question: How should files be named?
items.answer: Use clear, consistent names with project, language, track number, short title, and date. Keep originals safe and create clean copies when renaming.

items.question: What is an edited original?
items.answer: It is the cleaned version of the original recording before the final program is assembled. Keep originals, edited files, and final program files clearly separated.

items.question: Why check track duration?
items.answer: Duration helps with listener attention, program planning, video or picture timing, and sharing through apps, SD cards, or radio.

items.question: Can I use local songs or music?
items.answer: Only if permission is clear and the use is appropriate. Record who owns the song, who performed it, and where it may be shared.

items.question: Should we add intros and outros?
items.answer: Use simple intros/outros if they help listeners know what they are hearing and how to respond. Keep them short and natural.

items.question: What should I check before Program is complete?
items.answer: Check track order, audio quality, titles, speaker info, Scripture references, permissions, file names, and whether the program matches the ministry purpose.

items.question: What is package preview?
items.answer: Package preview shows the files and forms that will be submitted or shared so the team can catch missing items before handoff.

items.question: What does Submit mean?
items.answer: Submit means handing the finished package to the organization, reviewer, media team, database team, studio, or ministry office for review, publishing, archiving, or next steps.

items.question: What must be included in a submission package?
items.answer: Usually include audio files, scripts, translations or back-translations, consent, permissions, program/tracklist, metadata, notes, and review status.

items.question: Should I make a ZIP package?
items.answer: A ZIP package helps keep files together. Use a clear folder structure and check the package before sending.

items.question: What should reviewer notes include?
items.answer: Include what changed, what needs checking, unclear terms, technical concerns, missing permissions, and any cultural or theological questions.

items.question: What submission status should I use?
items.answer: Use Draft, Ready, Submitted, Needs Correction, Approved, or Published/Released. Keep it simple and update it when the handoff changes.

items.question: What if a large upload fails?
items.answer: Do not panic. Check internet, file size, package name, and whether resumable upload is available. If not, use physical drive, SD card, or alternate transfer approved by your team.

items.question: Can I submit if a permission is missing?
items.answer: Mark the package as not ready unless your organization allows review before permission is complete. Missing rights can block sharing later.

items.question: Why must metadata match the audio?
items.answer: Metadata helps others find, review, publish, and reuse the recording. If the form says one thing and the audio says another, the package may be delayed.

items.question: Should I back up before submitting?
items.answer: Yes. Keep a local copy of originals, edited files, final program, forms, and package before sending.

items.question: What happens after Submit?
items.answer: Track status, answer reviewer questions quickly, correct issues, and prepare for Share so the recording can reach listeners.

items.question: What does Share mean?
items.answer: Share means helping the finished message actually reach listeners through churches, believers, field workers, SD cards, Bluetooth, apps, QR codes, radio, speaker boxes, or listening groups.

items.question: How can we share offline?
items.answer: Use SD cards, USB drives, Bluetooth, phone-to-phone sharing, speaker boxes, local Wi-Fi sharing, printed QR cards where internet exists later, or listening groups.

items.question: How can we share online?
items.answer: Use an approved ministry website, app, QR link, messaging app, or cloud link. Confirm permissions before public online sharing.

items.question: What should the QR code point to?
items.answer: Point it to a stable page where listeners can access the audio in the right language. Test it on a phone before printing or sharing.

items.question: How should local churches be involved?
items.answer: Ask local churches how they can use the recording for evangelism, discipleship, children’s ministry, women’s ministry, listening groups, or follow-up.

items.question: What is a listening group plan?
items.answer: A listening group plan says who will gather listeners, where they meet, what they hear, who leads discussion, and how questions or responses will be followed up.

items.question: What feedback should we collect?
items.answer: Ask whether the language was understandable, the content was clear, people listened fully, questions came up, objections appeared, and more content is needed.

items.question: How should testimonies be recorded?
items.answer: Write or record testimonies with permission. Protect names and locations when public sharing could create risk.

items.question: How can it support children’s or women’s ministry?
items.answer: Plan age-appropriate listening settings, trusted facilitators, safe locations, and follow-up resources. Do not assume one sharing method fits everyone.

items.question: Why is Share a separate stage?
items.answer: Because a recording that is submitted but never reaches listeners has not yet fulfilled its ministry purpose. Share keeps distribution and follow-up visible.

items.question: Where do forms live?
items.answer: Each project has its own forms. Open Project Detail, then Forms, or open Forms & Checklists inside the stage you are working on.

items.question: When do I use Language & Community Profile?
items.answer: Use it during Research to describe the language, dialect, community, local verification, contacts, resources, and confidence level.

items.question: When do I use Recording Project Plan?
items.answer: Use it during Plan to organize purpose, audience, content, Scripture, speakers, helpers, equipment, travel, backup, and sharing plan.

items.question: When do I use Speaker & Helper Consent Form?
items.answer: Use it before recording anyone’s voice, song, photo, or name. Link it from Plan and Record.

items.question: When do I use Script & Content Approval?
items.answer: Use it when a script is drafted, translated, adapted, reviewed, or approved.

items.question: When do I use Recording Session Log?
items.answer: Use it during each recording session to record files, takes, problems, best take, playback, and backup.

items.question: When do I use Audio Program Form?
items.answer: Use it during Program to list the final program, track order, speakers, durations, notes, and file naming.

items.question: When do I use Rights & Permissions?
items.answer: Use it whenever content, music, scripts, photos, or voices may have restrictions. Show reminders in Plan, Program, and Submit.

items.question: When do I use Submission Package Checklist?
items.answer: Use it before Submit to confirm the package is complete and ready for handoff.

items.question: When do I use Field Feedback Form?
items.answer: Use it after Share to learn whether people understood, responded, raised concerns, or requested more content.

items.question: What roles should a Recording Team have?
items.answer: Use roles such as Research lead, Script lead, Speaker care, Recorder operator, Backup person, Editor, Reviewer, Submitter, and Distribution/Share lead. One person can hold more than one role, but the team should know who owns each task.

items.question: How do we avoid handoff confusion?
items.answer: At the end of each stage, assign who owns the next step, what is missing, and what must be reviewed. Write it down in the project notes.

items.question: Can Tailender Tom work offline?
items.answer: Yes, if this knowledge base is bundled with the PWA. Tom should search local JSON first and only use internet features when available.

items.question: What is Easy English mode?
items.answer: Easy English mode gives shorter, simpler answers for field workers using English as a second language.

items.question: How should I learn a stage?
items.answer: Use one short training card at a time: goal, why it matters, steps, common mistakes, and a quick practice task.

items.question: What should I do if I am not sure?
items.answer: Do not pretend. Mark the item Unknown, add a question, ask a trusted person, and keep the project moving only where it is safe.

items.question: What if device storage is full?
items.answer: Stop importing new files. Back up originals, remove duplicate exports, empty old temporary files, and keep the clean project package.

items.question: What if we have no internet?
items.answer: Use offline forms, local project data, saved training cards, and local audio files. Prepare a package that can be submitted later when connection is available.

items.question: What if I cannot find a file?
items.answer: Search by project, date, language, speaker, and recorder file name. Check originals, edited files, final program folder, backups, and memory card.

items.question: Why does the app still say Tailenders?
items.answer: Branding text is still in the code or manifest. Search for Tailenders, TAILENDERS, 67 RPM, and old icon paths, then replace with Tailender Tracks and 78 RPM.

items.question: I hear hum in the recording. What now?
items.answer: Check power cables, chargers, lights, fans, and nearby electronics. Try battery power, move cables away from audio lines, change location, and make a new test recording.

items.question: The speaker pops P and B sounds. What now?
items.answer: Move the microphone slightly off-axis, increase distance a little, use a pop filter or windscreen, and ask for natural speech, not forced projection.

items.question: The room sounds echoey. What now?
items.answer: Move to a smaller softer room, add blankets or curtains, avoid bare walls, and keep the mic closer to the speaker.

items.question: There are mouth clicks. What now?
items.answer: Give the speaker water, take breaks, avoid very dry mouth, and retake the line if clicks distract from the message.

items.question: What level should I record at?
items.answer: Aim for a strong clean level with safe headroom. Avoid peaks hitting the top/red. A clean lower recording is better than loud distorted audio.

items.question: The PWA opens blank. What should I do?
items.answer: Check the browser console, restart npm run dev, confirm src/main.tsx exists, and check that index.html points to /src/main.tsx.

items.question: The logo is missing. What should I check?
items.answer: Confirm the file exists in public/icons/tailender-buckle.png and the app uses /icons/tailender-buckle.png. Public files should not be referenced as src/ paths.

items.question: The PWA does not install. What should I check?
items.answer: Check manifest, service worker, HTTPS or localhost, valid icons, and browser console errors. Restart the dev server after manifest changes.

items.question: Git wants to commit a backup folder. What should I do?
items.answer: Do not commit temporary backup folders. Move them outside the repo, delete them after testing, or add them to .gitignore.

items.question: What is a good practice task for a trainee?
items.answer: Give a small project: confirm a language, choose a short script, record one clean sample, fill the session log, name files, and explain how it would be shared.
